meta.description: Non-inferable knowledge extracted from the five official CCA-P prep course modules: exact terms, values, behaviors, and definitions that must be memorized outright, plus counter-intuitive rules where the course answer contradicts common engineering intuition. items.sourceSection: What broke: a deterministic rule handed to a probabilistic system

points.v: Logging that catches a broken deterministic check (e.g. a SQL rule) doesn't record choices a model makes inside a request; a business rule folded into a probabilistic system drifts silently, surfacing only via manual audit

items.logic: Existing production monitoring is assumed to flag a broken business rule the way it flags a broken query.

items.sourceSection: Context-window sizing: the working-memory cliff

points.v: Budget largest realistic conversation + retrieved context + system prompt + working scratch + growth margin — never the full window

items.logic: Using as much of the advertised window as possible looks efficient, but designing toward the ceiling guarantees overflow in production.

items.sourceSection: Context strategy: spectrum between progressive and monolithic

points.v: Bounded tasks with predictable input size, stable prefixes for prompt caching, single-shot Q&A, reasoning needing simultaneous access to all material
As context accumulates turn over turn — cost and latency scale linearly with input length; attention quality can degrade before the hard limit

items.sourceSection: Context strategy: spectrum between progressive and monolithic

points.v: Stages context just-in-time — retrieve, summarize across turns, load only what the next step needs
"The right default for most production workloads"
Long-range coherence, decisions depending on detail dropped earlier, and prompt caching; the exact input seen at step N is no longer reconstructable

items.sourceSection: Context strategy: spectrum between progressive and monolithic

points.v: Long-running agents, phase transitions that can checkpoint to a clean summary, sessions that would otherwise hit context limits mid-task

Summaries drop load-bearing detail (identifiers, numeric values, prior decisions, edge cases); the summarizer is itself a model call, compaction is largely one-way, and summary fidelity is an unsolved eval problem

items.sourceSection: In practice, strategies may be combined

points.v: Context strategy (progressive vs monolithic, etc.) and context sizing are separate decisions that interact but don't determine each other

items.logic: Picking a strategy is assumed to settle how much context to budget; treating them as one is where most context designs go wrong.

items.sourceSection: The most common mistake: retrieval applied to live state

points.v: Stale chunks, results shifting with each index refresh, answers contradicting the database
Not a better embedding model or shorter refresh interval — call the system that owns the live state
High — the system looks healthy: normal latency, no errors

items.logic: Stale or contradictory results look like a retrieval-quality problem, but no refresh interval makes an index a source of live state.

items.sourceSection: How to decide if a problem needs one or several patterns

points.v: Reach for a second reference architecture only when the two parts of the problem break in different ways worth managing separately

Composing roughly doubles the surface area to maintain — when in doubt, pick one

items.topic: Guardrails belong in the output contract
items.sourceSection: Author the reusable prompt asset

points.v: Enforce a guardrail structurally by building it into the output contract as a constraint the format requires, not as a sentence in the role text
"A rule stated in the role can be drifted past. A constraint built into the output contract shapes the response format and cannot be quietly ignored."

items.logic: A forcefully worded prohibition in the role section reads like a real guardrail, but an instruction the model can route around is not a constraint.

items.sourceSection: Designing system prompts, templates, and guardrails

points.v: An underspecified guardrail is worse than a missing one, "because it creates the appearance of a control without the substance"
Underspecification — a gap the model fills with its own assumption, differently each time — is the named key failure in prompt design

items.logic: Partial protection seems strictly better than none, but the appearance of a control stops anyone from adding the real one.

items.sourceSection: Avoiding bias in prompt construction
items.lead: Prompt bias enters through three sources, answered by three disciplines

points.v: Fix: phrase neutrally
Fix: balance examples across the cases the system will see
Fix: check whether the prompt presumes the answer it should elicit
Bias is invisible in any single output and shows only in aggregate — a design requirement, not a polish step

items.sourceSection: What extended thinking controls

points.v: Run evals without extended thinking first; consider enabling it only if accuracy still misses requirements after working on the prompt

items.logic: It looks like a free quality upgrade, but without measured evidence you pay thinking tokens and latency on every call with no proof it moves accuracy.

points.v: A cost model built on average token usage can underestimate long-tail request cost by a factor of 2-3, since most requests are short but a tail consumes a disproportionate share of spend

items.logic: Sizing off observed average token count feels sound, but the average hides a tail that can double or triple real cost.

items.sourceSection: Data handling: what belongs in the context window

points.v: The context window is not a data-governance boundary — any data passed into a Claude call is transmitted to the API
Conversation content is not retained by default on the API, but the partner's own application layer typically logs requests; specific retention carve-outs exist

items.logic: Claude's default non-retention makes sensitive fields feel safe in the prompt, but the calling application's own request logging still captures everything sent.

items.sourceSection: Data handling: what belongs in the context window

points.v: For each field entering the context window, ask whether it's necessary for Claude to produce the intended output

Reference identifiers (account numbers, claim numbers) are often needed for routing but not for the language task — passing the full data field when the identifier suffices exposes it to application-layer logging without adding capability

items.sourceSection: Observability: what to log, what to trace, and why

points.v: Without a trustworthy audit trail, an autonomous system is not approved to act — security reviewers treat observability as the precondition for enabling agents, and an agentic action taken but not logged is treated as one that cannot be allowed

items.sourceSection: Observability: what to log, what to trace, and why

points.v: Separate API keys per tenant are required for attribution and isolation in any production multi-tenant deployment — on a shared key, an org-level rate-limit breach is visible but can't be attributed to the tenant that caused it, and every tenant absorbs the impact

items.sourceSection: Observability: what to log, what to trace, and why

items.sourceSection: Reading results without overclaiming

points.v: LLM experiments have a failure mode classical A/B tests don't: interaction effects between the treatment and specific input types — a prompt change that improves typical inputs can degrade rare edge cases that appear frequently in a later seasonal spike
Test-period and input-distribution alignment matter more here than in most other software contexts

items.sourceSection: Shadow testing: validating a change before any user sees it

points.v: Use when deployment can absorb small bounded exposure to a worse version and traffic is high enough for a meaningful sample in a reasonable window
Use when a single bad output carries too much risk or traffic is too low to split

Shadow testing costs downstream signal — scoring relies on an offline rubric or golden answers rather than real user behavior — and is often the only acceptable validation method in regulated-industry deployments

points.v: Trained refusals cover broad, general-purpose harm only
A deployment-specific rule (e.g. no cross-business-unit record access) never encoded in a classifier, system prompt, or application control is simply unenforced
A normal-looking, in-domain request for a forbidden record then gets answered

items.logic: Reliable refusal of harmful prompts in testing suggests safety training generalizes to your domain access rules, but it never saw them.

items.topic: One output filter is not a guarded path
items.sourceSection: When a single output filter looks like a finished design

points.v: An output filter inspects only generated text and runs after a tool call has already executed
A model that calls a refund tool completes the irreversible financial action before screening happens
Side-effecting tool calls need their own authorization gate before execution

items.logic: Output filtering looks like the decisive control because it sits closest to the user and is easiest to point to on a diagram.

items.sourceSection: Fail open versus fail closed: how your guardrail layer behaves under failure

points.v: Absent an explicit choice, a guardrail that errors under load or becomes unreachable lets requests through unscreened — fail open

items.logic: Reliability instinct says degrade gracefully and keep serving rather than block legitimate users.

items.sourceSection: When routing everything to review makes review meaningless

points.v: Sending every output to a person with only the output and an approve button collapses into rubber-stamping once volume exceeds reading capacity
High-stakes decisions get the same approval as trivial ones
Two failures stack: volume beyond capacity, and missing context to judge against

items.logic: Routing everything to a human feels like the maximally conservative default that needs no judgment about stakes.

items.sourceSection: Build the review-routing rule

points.v: Confidence is not one of the two deciding controls for routing (reversibility and cost of a wrong answer are)
A confident case still routes to a human if irreversible or high-cost
Confidence estimates only how likely the output is wrong, not what happens if it is

items.logic: The natural design is 'low confidence to a human, high confidence through', treating confidence as the primary routing signal.

items.sourceSection: What the reviewer sees decides whether review is accurate

The better pattern is monitoring with intervention, concentrating review at higher-value checkpoints such as plan review or exception handling
This is the reasoning behind plan-level review in Claude Code, where a person approves the plan rather than each step

items.logic: Approving every single agent action seems maximally cautious, but it induces consent fatigue and lowers real oversight.
